title: Introduction to an Operating System (Linux and UNIX Commands)
learningGoals: Explain what an OS is (a resource manager and an interface between the user and the hardware), the layered design, system calls, and terminal vs shell vs kernel.
Compare GUI vs CLI and know when each fits.
Pass data to a C program through command-line arguments ( argv , atoi , atof ).
Use the basic commands: ls , pwd , cd , mkdir , passwd , man , info , date , cal .
Use the file and text commands: cat , cp , mv , rm , chmod , redirection, wc , sort , head , tail , grep , find , pipes and tee .
Explain inodes, hard links vs symbolic links, and basic process commands ( & , jobs , ps , kill ).
sirStressed: "Today's goal is not memorisation, it's exploration." "We will never test you on how many commands or options you remember." You need the concepts: what the CLI is, where and why to use it, and how commands combine.
The command line is a mandatory skill (AI servers, the cloud, GPUs, Docker). "Command line is not old. Command line is power."
Which interface fits the task? That's the right question, and sir called it very important.
Terminal ≠ OS, shell ≠ kernel. Commands become processes that make system calls.
. is the current directory and .. is the parent. Practise them.
Quizzes are multiple choice. Assessment components are quizzes + assignment + exams = 100 marks. Quiz 1 covered modules 1–3.
commonTraps: > overwrites while >> appends. << is a here-document, not "append input".
ls > op | wc prints 0, because the output already went to the file.
grep searches contents; find searches file names/attributes. grep -c counts lines; wc -l counts lines of any input.
chmod digit order is user, group, others, and r = 4, w = 2, x = 1.
Hard links can't point to directories, and they survive deletion of the original. Symlinks break.
argv[0] is the program name, not the first user argument.
uniq needs sorted input. head -n 1 keeps the first line.
cp keeps the source and mv removes it. rm -i prompts for each file; rm -I prompts once.
summary: OS = resource manager and interface between user and hardware. Layered (hardware = layer 0). Abstracts the hardware. In UNIX, everything is a file; you deal with files and processes.
You → terminal → shell → program/process → system calls → kernel → hardware. Apps use APIs and libraries that wrap system calls.
GUI is visual and one-off. CLI is precise, repetitive, remote and automatable. Ctrl+Alt+T opens a terminal.
argv[0] = program name; all arguments are strings; atoi and atof stop at the first invalid character.
Navigation: pwd , ls (-a -A -l -h -R -t -S -r -1), cd ( cd , cd .. ), mkdir -p , absolute vs relative paths.
passwd (-l lock, -u unlock, -d delete, -e expire). man (sections 1–9) is crisp; info is detailed and hyperlinked. date (-u, -s, -d), cal (-j Julian, -m Monday).
cat , cp (copy), mv (cut/rename), rm (-i -I -r -f), chmod 755/644, u+x.
Redirection > , >> , < , << , 2> . Filters wc (-l -w -c -m -L), sort (-n -r -M -h -u -c -m -o), head / tail (10 lines by default, -n, tail -f ).
grep (-i -v -w -x -c -n -l -o -r -E -F), find (-name -type f/d/l -mtime). Pipes | (FIFO), tee , sort | uniq .
Inode = metadata. Hard link = same inode, files only, survives deletion. Symlink = shortcut, works for directories too, can dangle.

questions.prompt: The operating system acts as a ______.
questions.explanation: the OS manages the CPU, memory, I/O and files. That's the lecture's key definition.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a general-purpose OS?
questions.explanation: VxWorks is a real-time/embedded OS, Sprite was a research distributed OS, and iOS is tied to Apple's mobile devices. Linux runs everything from servers to desktops.

questions.prompt: Which is true of the command-line interface?

options.text: Very efficient for connecting to remote systems

questions.explanation: a CLI works over SSH with tiny bandwidth, which makes remote work easy. Ease of use and friendliness are GUI strengths.

questions.prompt: Which shortcut opens a terminal in Linux?
questions.explanation: "T" for Terminal. Ctrl+Alt+L locks the screen.

questions.prompt: A program is run as ./a.out Hi 5 . What is argv[0] ?
questions.explanation: argv[0] is the program name exactly as typed, including ./ . argv[1] = "Hi" and argv[2] = "5" (a string!).
topicTags: Taking Different Datatypes from the Command Line

questions.prompt: What does atoi("12abc34") return?
questions.explanation: atoi converts digits until the first non-digit character and then stops.
topicTags: Taking Different Datatypes from the Command Line

questions.prompt: Which ls option sorts files by modification time?
questions.explanation: -t = time (newest first). -r only reverses the order.

questions.prompt: Which ls option shows inode numbers?
questions.explanation: -i = inode. That's useful for checking whether two names are hard links (same inode).

questions.prompt: Which cd option goes back to the previous working directory?
questions.explanation: cd - toggles to the last directory. .. = parent, / = root, ~ = home.

questions.prompt: Which passwd option makes an account passwordless?
questions.explanation: -d = delete the password. ( -l locks and -u unlocks.)

questions.prompt: Which man command shows exit as a system call?
questions.explanation: man section 1 = user commands, 2 = system calls, 3 = library functions.

questions.prompt: Which command is best for exploring related topics?
questions.explanation: info pages are hyperlinked, so you can jump between related nodes. man is crisp but flat.

questions.prompt: Which command displays the date from some months ago? (The quiz stem says "2 months ago" but its marked option says "3 months ago". The quiz has a typo.)
questions.explanation: date -d / --date="N months ago" prints a relative date. It's the only option that does this. For 2 months you'd write date --date="2 months ago" .

questions.prompt: Which cal option shows Julian dates for the previous, current and next months?
questions.explanation: -j = Julian day numbers, and -3 = the three months. Combined, that's -j3 .

questions.prompt: Which command concatenates file1.txt, then text typed by the user, then file2.txt?
questions.explanation: a lone - means "read standard input here". Type your text, then press Ctrl+D.

questions.prompt: Which cp option creates hard links instead of copying?
questions.explanation: -l = link (hard). -i = interactive prompt. -H / -L are about following symlinks.

questions.prompt: Which mv option prompts before overwriting?
questions.explanation: -i = interactive, so it asks before overwriting. -n = no-clobber: it silently never overwrites and doesn't prompt. -f forces and -u updates only if the source is newer. The quiz marked both B and C. B is the real answer, worked out.
topicTags: File Processing Commands: mv, rm, chmod

questions.prompt: file1.txt has read permission for user, group and other ( r--r--r-- ). Change it to read+execute for user, read for group, and nothing for other.
questions.explanation: the target is r-xr----- (octal 540). Add x for the user and remove r from others, both at once. 740 would be rwxr----- (it adds write, which is wrong).
topicTags: File Processing Commands: mv, rm, chmod

questions.prompt: What does cat < file1.txt > file2.txt do?

options.text: Takes input from file1.txt and directs it to file2.txt
Takes input from file2.txt and shows it
Takes input from file1.txt and shows it

questions.explanation: < feeds file1 as input and > sends the output into file2. It's effectively a copy.

questions.prompt: Which redirection appends to a file?
questions.explanation: >> appends and > overwrites. << is a here-document (input).

questions.prompt: Which command lists hidden files but not . and .. ?
questions.explanation: -A is "almost all": hidden files, but without . and .. .

questions.prompt: After chmod 640 report.txt , which statement is true?

options.text: Owner can read and write; group can read; others have no access

questions.explanation: 6 = rw (owner), 4 = r (group), 0 = none (others).

questions.prompt: You delete file1.txt , which had a hard link h1.txt and a symbolic link s1.txt . What happens?

options.text: h1.txt still shows the content; s1.txt becomes dangling

questions.explanation: A hard link shares the inode, so the data stays until the link count reaches 0. A symlink stores only the path, so it dangles.

questions.prompt: Output of ls > op | wc :
questions.explanation: The ls output went to the file op , so wc reads empty input.

questions.prompt: Which command counts how many lines of app.log contain "ERROR"?
questions.explanation: grep -c counts matching lines. ( -v inverts the match.)

questions.prompt: In ./a.out 45 hello , what is argv[1] ?
questions.explanation: All arguments are strings. argv[0] is ./a.out and argv[1] is "45" ; convert it with atoi .

questions.prompt: Write one pipeline that shows the 3 most frequent distinct lines in server.log that contain "ERROR", with their counts.
correctAnswers: grep ERROR server.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -3
questions.explanation: grep ERROR server.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -3

questions.prompt: Give two differences between man and info .
correctAnswers: man is crisp and gives a flat page per command with sections 1–9. info is more detailed, hierarchical and hyperlinked, easier to navigate, and exportable to HTML or PDF. It's better for learning a tool in depth.
questions.explanation: man is crisp and gives a flat page per command with sections 1–9. info is more detailed, hierarchical and hyperlinked, easier to navigate, and exportable to HTML or PDF. It's better for learning a tool in depth.

questions.prompt: Scenario: your training job runs on a headless cloud server abroad. Which interface do you use, and why?
correctAnswers: The CLI over SSH. The server is remote and headless, a CLI needs far less bandwidth than a GUI, and it's precise and scriptable for repeated jobs.
questions.explanation: The CLI over SSH. The server is remote and headless, a CLI needs far less bandwidth than a GUI, and it's precise and scriptable for repeated jobs.

questions.prompt: What is an inode, and what does it contain?
correctAnswers: An inode is the metadata block (file control block) of a file or directory, identified by an inode number. It holds the size, data-block locations, permissions, owner and group, and the created, modified and accessed times. It doesn't hold the file name.
questions.explanation: An inode is the metadata block (file control block) of a file or directory, identified by an inode number. It holds the size, data-block locations, permissions, owner and group, and the created, modified and accessed times. It doesn't hold the file name.
